title.rendered: Rustic Star Granny Square

content.rendered:
There is something undeniably enchanting about rustic crochet designs. They bring to mind cozy cabin retreats, flannel blankets, and crisp autumn evenings by the fire. If you are looking to capture that same warm, inviting aesthetic in your next project, this Rustic Star Granny Square is the perfect pattern for you.

This pattern stands out from traditional flat granny squares by utilizing a brilliant combination of dimensional bobbles and multi-toned color changes. The result is a highly textured, raised star motif that practically pops right off the fabric. The unique construction—particularly the way the star points are formed by encasing chains—creates a thick, cozy fabric that feels as luxurious as it looks.

Because this pattern involves some non-traditional techniques like creating puffs with incomplete half double crochets and working stitches over chains, it is a fantastic project for intermediate crocheters looking to expand their skillset. If you are a visual learner, be sure to watch the step-by-step video tutorial to see exactly how these beautiful star points come to life before diving into the written instructions below!

Materials Needed

  • Yarn of your choice- 4 colors; the sample is made with wool yarn.
  • Crochet hook- we are using a 3.00mm hook
  • Darning Needle
  • Scissors

Pattern Notes

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology.

Working with multiple colors and dimensional stitches requires a bit of attention to detail. In this pattern, you will be creating “3-hdc-puff” stitches. Unlike a traditional puff stitch made with double crochets, this pattern creates dense, rustic-textured puffs by working 3 incomplete half double crochets into the same stitch, then yarn over and pulling through all the loops on your hook at once.

You will also encounter a unique technique in Round 6 where you are asked to work stitches “while encasing the chain above.” This means you will be pushing your hook through the stitches of the previous round and looping your working yarn over the loose chain from the prior round, trapping it inside your new stitches. This is the secret to getting that gorgeous, raised 3D effect on the star points!

Pattern Instructions

Creating the Center & Bobbles

Round 1 Magic ring, ch2(count as hdc), 15hdc, slst to the top of the first ch2, fasten off.

Round 2 Join new yarn to any st, ch1, 3 incomplete hdc in this st, yo and pull through all loops to form 3-hdc-puff. 3-hdc-puff in remaining sts, slst to the first puff.

Round 3 With white yarn, ch3(count as dc)+2dc. with blue yarn, 3dc in next st. [with white yarn, (3dc). with blue yarn, (3dc)] rep 7 times. slst to the top of the first ch3, fasten off.

Round 4 Join new yarn to any st, ch1, 1sc in each st, slst to the first sc.

Forming the Star Points

Round 5 ch2(count as incomplete dc)+2 incomplete dc to form an incomplete 3-dc-bo. sk3. make an incomplete 3-dc-bo in next st, yo and pull through all loops to complete a 3-dc-bo2tog, ch7. sk1, make a 3-dc-bo2tog over the next and 5th st (skipping 3 sts between). ch7 rep 7 times, slst to the first dec, fasten off.

Round 6 Pull new yarn up from the gap under a dec, ch4(count as tr)+2tr. Work into the skipped st under next chain: make 4tr while encasing the chain above. ch1, sk next dec, 4tr in next skipped st while encasing the chain above, 3tr+ch2 in the gap under next dec. [3tr in the current gap, 4tr in next skipped st while encasing the chain above. ch1, sk next dec, 4tr in next skipped st while encasing the chain above, 3tr+ch2 in the gap under next dec] rep 3 times, slst to the top of the first ch4, fasten off.

The Rustic Border

Round 7 Join brown yarn to any corner, ch2(count as hdc)+1hdc. 7hdc. Work into the gap under the skipped dec with orange yarn: 3-dc-bo while encasing the chain above. with brown yarn, 7hdc, 2hdc+ch2. [still in brown yarn, 2hdc in the current corner, 7hdc. Work into the gap under the skipped dec with orange yarn: 3-dc-bo while encasing the chain above. with brown yarn, 7hdc, 2hdc+ch2]rep 3 times, slst to the top of the first ch2.

Round 8 ch1, sc in each st, 2sc+ch1+2sc in each corner. slst to the first sc, fasten off.

Design & Texture Tips

To truly get that “rustic” feel, the type of yarn you choose makes a massive difference. As suggested in the materials list, wool yarn is the perfect choice for this specific pattern. Wool has a natural fuzziness (often called a “halo”) that softens the harsh lines of the color changes and makes the dimensional bobbles look incredibly plush and cozy. If you are sensitive to wool or prefer a vegan alternative, a high-quality tweed or roving-style acrylic yarn will give you a similar textured, rustic appearance.

Blocking is also highly recommended for this square. Because you are working treble crochets and bobbles on one side, and single crochets on the other, the square may want to curl or pucker slightly. Gently wet-blocking or steam-blocking the square and pinning it out to perfect right angles will make joining your squares together infinitely easier later on.

More Fun Granny Square Patterns

If you loved the 3D, textured element of this rustic star, you will absolutely adore our 3D Christmas tree granny square pattern, which uses a similar layered puff stitch technique to create a raised holiday tree.

For more seasonal motifs, we have plenty of options! You can crochet a beautiful Christmas star granny square featuring a stunning lacy 5-pointed star. And if you like to get a little spooky when the weather cools down, be sure to check out our spooky ghost granny square and the edgy, highly detailed skull and flower granny square.

Conclusion

Congratulations on completing your Rustic Star Granny Square! This highly textured, multi-toned star design is a true showstopper that will bring warmth and dimension to any crochet project. Share your cozy creations in the comments below!

title.rendered: 3D Christmas Tree Granny Square

content.rendered:
The holiday season brings out the best in the crochet community, inspiring us to create cozy, festive projects that spread cheer. If you are looking for a show-stopping motif to add to your winter decor, this 3D Christmas Tree Granny Square is exactly what you need. Unlike flat, color-work squares, this pattern features a beautifully raised Christmas tree crafted entirely with layered puff stitches, giving it a stunning, tactile texture that truly pops.

This pattern brilliantly combines a standalone 3D tree motif with a traditional, striped granny square background. The contrast between the textured, popped-out tree and the smooth, solid square creates a professional-looking design that is surprisingly beginner-friendly. Whether you are making a holiday blanket, a festive pillow cover, or a simple winter wall hanging, this square is guaranteed to be a conversation starter. If you love exploring different textured square designs, you might also enjoy this cluster crochet granny square pattern for another unique 3D effect!

Materials Needed

  • Yarn of your choice- 4 colors (We recommend a classic green for the tree, brown for the trunk, white for the inner background, and a festive color like red or gold for the outer border)
  • Crochet hook
  • Darning Needle
  • Scissors

Abbreviations Used

  • ch – chain
  • st(s) – stitch(es)
  • hdc – half double crochet
  • dc – double crochet
  • sl st – slip stitch
  • puff – puff stitch
  • dec – decrease
  • rep – repeat

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology.

Tips for Success

Before diving into the pattern, there are a few helpful techniques to keep in mind. This design utilizes a specific method for creating puffs using incomplete half double crochet stitches. Rather than the traditional yarn-over puff stitch, you will be making incomplete hdc stitches and pulling the yarn through all loops at once to create a dense, highly textured fabric. This is what gives the tree its incredible 3D, raised appearance.

Additionally, the background square relies on “invisible standing stitches.” This technique allows you to start a new round or color without the bulky, visible knot of a traditional chain start, resulting in a seamless, professional finish. If you are new to this method, simply practice creating an incomplete stitch and pulling your loop up to the height of a regular stitch before proceeding.

Note: When assembling, take your time to pin the tree motif centrally onto the square before sewing to ensure your stitches are evenly spaced and the tree sits perfectly straight.

If you love working with textured, raised stitches like this, you will absolutely adore our bobble stitch pumpkin pattern for your fall crafting. For more traditional square constructions, our granny square crochet pattern diagram is a fantastic visual resource to keep in your bookmarks!

Pattern Instructions

The Tree Body

Row 1 – knot, ch9, work into the 2nd st from the end, the last chain we skipped is counted as an incomplete hdc, make another 2 incomplete hdc in this ch to form a 3-hdc-puff, 3-hdc-puff in the next chrep 7 times.

Row 2 – turn over, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make another incomplete hdc in this st, then make two incomplete hdc in the next st, yo pull through al loop s on your hook, forming a 2-hdc-puff dec over these two sts, 3-hdc-puff in each of the next 4 sts, 2-hdc puff dec over next 2 puff sts.

Row 3 – turn over, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make another incomplete hdc in this st, then make two incomplete hdc in the next st, yo, pull through all loops on your hook, forming a 2-hdc-puff dec over these two sts, 3-hdc-puff in each of the next 2 sts, 2-hdc-puff dec over next 2 puff sts.

Row 4 – turn over, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make another incomplete hdc in this st to form a 2-hdc-puff, 3-hdc-puff dec over following 2 puff sts, 2-hdc-puff in next puff st.

Row 5 – turn over, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make another incomplete hdc in this st to form a 3-hdc-puff, 3-hdc-puff in each of the next 2 puff sts.

Row 6 – turn over, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make 2 incomplete hdc in this st, make 3 incomplete hdc in each of the next 2 sts, yo, pull through all loops on the hook, forming a 3-hdc-puff dec over 3 sts, weave in ends.

The Trunk

Upside down, add new yarn to the 4th st from right, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make another incomplete hdc in this st to form a 2-hdc-puff, 2-hdc-puff in next st, turn over, ch(count as an incomplete hdc), make another incomplete hdc in this st to form a 2-hdc-puff, 2-hdc-puff in the next st, sl st to the top of the first puff, fasten off.

The Square

Round 1 – Start with a magic loop, ch1 as a standing st, 1 invisible standing st (count as 1dc),3dc in the loop, ch3, [4dc, ch3] repeat 3 times, sl st to the invisible standing st.

Round 2 – ch1 as a standing st, 1 invisible standing st (count as 1hdc), hdc in the following 3 sts, 2hdc ch2 2hdc in the corner space.[1hdc in the next 4 sts, 2hdc ch2 2hdc in the corner space] repeat 3 times, sl st to the invisible standing st.

Round 3 – ch1 as a standing st, 1 invisible standing st (count as 1dc), dc in the following 5 sts, 2dc ch2 2dc in the corner space, 1hdc in the next 2 sts.[1dc in the next 6 sts, 2dc ch2 2dc in the corner space, 1hdc in the next 2 sts] repeat 3 times, sl st to the first invisible standing st, fasten off.

Round 4 – add new yarn into any corner sp, ch3(count as dc), dc ch3 2dc in this corner space, 12dc.[2dc ch3 2dc in the corner space, 12dc] repeat 3 times, sl st to the top of the first ch3, fasten off.

Round 5 – add new yarn into any corner sp, ch3(count as dc), dc ch3 2dc in this corner space, 16dc.[2dc ch3 2dc in the corner space, 16dc] repeat 3 times, sl st to the top of the first ch3, fasten off.

Assembly

Join the Christmas tree motif to the solid granny square background.

FAQ

Can I make this square larger? Absolutely! To make a larger square, simply continue the pattern logic of the final rounds. You would add a round of single crochets evenly around the perimeter, followed by additional rounds of double crochets with chain-3 corners, increasing your side stitches until you reach your desired size.

What is the best yarn to use for 3D stitches? A worsted weight (size 4) acrylic or cotton blend yarn is highly recommended for this pattern. Acrylic yarn has excellent “memory” which helps the 3D puff stitches hold their popped-out shape without flopping over. Cotton blends also work beautifully and give the square a lovely, structured drape.

How do I care for a 3D textured blanket? When washing projects made with heavily textured 3D stitches, it is best to hand wash or use a gentle machine cycle in cold water. Lay the item flat to dry to prevent the weighted puff stitches from stretching or losing their dimensional shape under gravity.

Conclusion

Congratulations on completing your 3D Christmas Tree Granny Square! This beautifully textured, raised design is a unique and festive way to celebrate the holiday season. Share your finished square in the comments below!

title.rendered: Christmas Star Granny Square

content.rendered:
The holiday season is the perfect time to start crocheting heartfelt, handmade gifts. If you are looking for festive Christmas gift ideas, don’t miss this stunning Christmas star granny square! Featuring a lovely 5-pointed star in the center, this design brings an open, lacy feel to your projects that is simply breathtaking.

This pattern takes the classic concept of a twinkle star and elevates it with a larger, more detailed motif that really pops. It is a fantastic project for crocheters looking to expand their granny square skills. If you love collecting square patterns as much as we do, be sure to explore our offset granny square pattern or try something unique like the hexagon granny square for even more crafting fun!

Materials Needed

  • Yarn of your choice- 2 colors
  • Crochet hook- We are using a 3.00mm hook
  • Darning Needle for weaving the ends
  • Scissors

Abbreviations Used

  • bo – bobble stitch
  • ch – chain stitch
  • ch-sp – chain space
  • dc – double crochet
  • tr – treble crochet
  • hdc – half double crochet
  • rep – repeat
  • st – stitch
  • sc – single crochet
  • slst/sl st – slip stitch
  • yo – yarn over
  • tl – third loop
  • TLO – Third loop only

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology.

Finished Size

The finished Christmas Star granny square is about 4.13 inches by 4.13 inches.

Pattern Instructions

Creating the Star

Round 1: Knot on your hook, ch5, sl st to the first ch to form a circle.

Round 2: ch2 as a standing st(count as an incomplete dc), make another 2 incomplete dc in this circle, yo and pull through all loops on your hook to form a 3-dc-bo, ch3. [3-dc-bo+ch3 in this circle] rep 4 times, sl st to the top of the first bo.

Make ch2 as a standing st(count as an incomplete dc).

make another 2 incomplete dc in this circle, yo and pull through all loops on your hook to form a 3-dc-bo, ch3.

[3-dc-bo+ch3 in this circle] rep 4 times, sl st to the top of the first bo.

Round 3: ch3 as standing st(count as a dc), (2dc+ch3+3dc) in the same st. (3dc+ch3+3dc) in next bo rep 4 times, sl st to the top of the first ch3.

ch3 as standing st(count as a dc).

(2dc+ch3+3dc) in the same st.

(3dc+ch3+3dc) in next borep 4 times, sl st to the top of the first ch3.

Round 4: ch1 as a standing st, 1sc in this st, ch1, (3dc+ch3+3dc) in next ch-sp, ch1. 1sc in the gap between following two 3-dc group, ch1, (3dc+ch3+3dc) in next ch-sp, ch1 rep 4 times. sl st to the top of the first sc, fasten off.

ch1 as a standing st.

1sc in this st, ch1, (3dc+ch3+3dc) in next ch-sp, ch1.

1sc in the gap between following two 3-dc group, ch1, (3dc+ch3+3dc) in next ch-sp, ch1 rep 4 times. sl st to the top of the first sc, fasten off.

Squaring the Circle

From this point forward, we will work exclusively in the third loop. This technique hugs our star center without disturbing those beautiful points, then gradually transforms our star into a square.

Round 5: TLO for this Round. Join new yarn to the third loop(tl) of the middle ch in any ch-3 group. ch1, 1sc in this st, 1hdc, 1dc, 5tr, 1dc, 1hdc, 1sc. [sl st to the next st, 1sc in next st, 1hdc, 1dc, 5tr, 1dc, 1hdc, 1sc] rep 4 times, sl st to the first ch1, fasten off.

TLO for this Round. Join new yarn to the third loop(tl) of the middle ch in any ch-3 group.

ch1.

Round 6: ch2 as a standing st(count as 1hdc). 1hdc, 4sc, 2hdc, 2dc, 1tr, (1tr+ch2+1tr) in next st, 1tr, 2dc. 2hdc, 4sc, 2hdc, 2dc, 1tr, (1tr+ch2+1tr) in next st, 1tr, 2dc rep 3 times, sl st to the top of the first ch2.

ch2 as a standing st(count as 1hdc).

1hdc, 4sc, 2hdc, 2dc, 1tr, (1tr+ch2+1tr) in next st, 1tr, 2dc.

2hdc, 4sc, 2hdc, 2dc, 1tr, (1tr+ch2+1tr) in next st, 1tr, 2dc rep 3 times, sl st to the top of the first ch2.

Round 7: ch1 to start, 1sc in this st, 1sc in each remaining st, while (1sc+ch2+1sc) in each corner sp, finally sl st to the top of the first sc, fasten off.

If you enjoyed making this festive motif, you might also love the free ombre granny square pattern for a modern gradient look, or the skull and flower granny square for a fun, edgy twist on traditional designs.

Conclusion

Congratulations on completing your Christmas Star Granny Square! This beautiful, lacy star design is a fantastic way to add festive charm to your holiday gifts and decor. Share your finished squares in the comments below!

title.rendered: Easy Crochet Bandana Pattern

content.rendered:
There is nothing quite like a quick, stylish crochet project to kick off the spring and summer seasons! This easy crochet bandana is incredibly versatile—you can make one for yourself, gift it to a friend, or even size it down to create an adorable crochet dog bandana pattern. It is the perfect grab-and-go project to toss in your bag for road trips or lazy evenings catching up on your favorite shows.

Using a lightweight cotton yarn, this bandana scarf is wonderfully cool and breathable for warmer weather. Whether you are a beginner looking for a fun introduction to shell stitches or an experienced crocheter wanting a relaxing, stash-busting make, this pattern is sure to become a favorite. Watch the full video tutorial here to see exactly how it comes together!

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology.

Materials Needed

  • 1 skein of cotton worsted weight yarn
  • 5.00 mm crochet hook
  • Large eye needle
  • Scissors

Abbreviations Used

  • Ch = Chain
  • Sc = Single Crochet
  • Dc = Double Crochet
  • Sl st = Slip Stitch
  • St = Stitch

Pattern Instructions

Special Stitches

Magic loop: wrap yarn around hand, insert hook into loop and pull up a loop. Remove your hand from the loop, chain 3 and begin pattern.

Shell stitch: 5 dc in space, sl st in center dc of next granny cluster.

Gauge & Size

  • Gauge: 4 granny clusters = 4″.
  • Finished Size: approx. 18″ across (not counting ties) and approx. 10″ long

Notes

  • Chain 3 counts as first double crochet in every row

Bandana Body

Row 1: Make a magic loop. Ch 3 (counts as first st), then (2 dc, ch 1, 3 dc) in loop.

Pull short end of yarn to tighten. Turn.

Row 2: Ch 3, 2 dc into same st, (3 dc, ch 1, 3 dc) in corner space, 3 dc in top of ch 3. Turn.

Row 3: Ch 3, 2 dc into same st. 3 dc in next space. (3 dc, ch 1, 3 dc) in corner space. 3 dc in next space. 3 dc in top of ch 3. Turn.

Row 4 – 13: Ch 3, 2 dc into same st. 3 dc in all spaces along first side. (3 dc, ch 1, 3 dc) in corner ch space. 3 dc in all spaces along this side. 3 dc in top of ch 3. Turn.

Leave yarn attached for next part.

Scalloped Edge

Ch 1, sk first dc, sl st into next dc.

Make 5 dc in space. Sl st into center dc of 3 dc cluster. Repeat to corner.

Make 7 dc into corner space, then continue 5 dc scallop pattern down the other side.

Last sl st will be in st right before ch 3 of previous row. Leave yarn attached for next part.

Ties

Ch 61. Sk first ch, sl st into 2nd ch from hook and each sl st down the row.

Sc in same st that tie is attached to. Sc evenly down the straight side of bandana until you reach the other side.

I made 55 sc, but yours may vary. Note: If you sc over the yarn end from the magic loop, you won’t have to weave it in later!

Ch 61. Sk first ch, sl st into 2nd ch from hook and each sl st down the row.

Sl st into side of st at base of tie.

Finish off. Weave in ends and trim off excess. Done!

Tips

  • Yarn Selection: The sample uses a worsted weight cotton yarn (“I Love This Cotton” in “Rosey” from Hobby Lobby), which works beautifully. Cotton is highly recommended for this pattern because it is cool, breathable, and perfect for warm spring and summer weather.
  • Stash Buster: You will only need one skein of yarn for this project—and you likely won’t even use the whole ball! It is a fantastic way to use up random leftover yarn from your stash.
  • Yarn Substitution Warning: You can use any worsted weight yarn you like, but keep in mind that acrylic yarn stretches out significantly more than cotton yarn will over time.

If you love this style, you’ll also enjoy this Modern Crochet Bandana Pattern That Feels Fresh & Minimal or this beautiful Boho Lace Floral Crochet Bandana Pattern.

FAQ

Can I make this as a dog bandana? Absolutely! This is a highly versatile pattern. You can easily adjust the starting chain or stop crocheting earlier to create the perfect size for your furry friend. If you’re making pet accessories, you might also love this Daisy Granny Square Hair Kerchief Pattern.

How do I adjust the size? To make it smaller or larger, simply add or subtract rows before working the scalloped edge. Just remember that changing the size will alter how much yarn you need for the foundation and ties.

What if my scallops look uneven? Count your stitches carefully as you go. Making sure you have exactly 3 double crochets in each space along the sides, and 7 in the corners, will keep your edges perfectly uniform. For even more bandana inspiration, check out this collection of 18 Free Crochet Bandana Patterns for Beginners.

Conclusion

Congratulations on finishing your beautiful crochet bandana! This lightweight, scalloped design makes a perfect breezy accessory for warmer weather. Share your finished bandana (or dog bandana!) in the comments below!

title.rendered: Spooky Ghost Granny Square

content.rendered:
Get ready for the spookiest season of the year with a hauntingly cute addition to your crochet queue! This ghost granny square features a classic white phantom floating against a deep black background, capturing that perfect Halloween vibe with its expressive little face and wavy shape.

Don’t be spooked by the colorwork—this pattern is surprisingly beginner-friendly. Using only basic stitches like single and double crochet, it is a fantastic way to practice color changes and textured shaping on a smaller scale before tackling a massive project.

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology.

Materials Needed

  • Yarn of your choice (2 colors)
  • Crochet hook (3.00mm hook used in the sample)
  • Darning needle
  • Scissors

Abbreviations Used

  • ch = chain stitch
  • dc = double crochet
  • sc = single crochet
  • st = stitch
  • Sl St = slip stitch for joining for different round
  • BLO = back loop only

Pattern Instructions

Round 1: Start with knot, ch5, 1 sc in the back loop of each of the 4th, 3rd, 2nd chains. 2sc In the back loop of the 1st chain, then 2 sc in the front loop of the same stitch. 1 sc in the front loop of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th chains, sl st to the 5th chain.

Round 2: ch, 1sc in the 5th chain, 2sc in the next st, sc in the following 3 sts, 3dc in the following 2 sts, sc, sc, sl st in the next 4 sts.

Round 3: Start from the st you made the last sl st in the previous round, sc, 2dc, ch2, sl st to the next st, sc in the following 5 sts, 2dc in the following 4 sts, sc in the following 7 sts, then 3sc, sc dc, 2dc, ch2, sc in the next 4 sts, dc, dc.

Round 4: ch1, flip the workpiece, sc in the same st, sl st in the next 6 sts, sc dc in the next st, ch, sl st to the same st, sl st in the next 12 sts. Flip the workpiece, ch3, dc, sc, sl st to the next st, fasten off.

Round 5: BLO. Add new yarn in the back loop of the fifth dc from right to left, ch as a standing st, 2sc in the same st, 2sc in the following 3 sts, sc, 3dc, sc, 2sc, sc in the following 23 sts, 3dc, sc, 2sc in the next 3 sts, sl st to the first ch.

Round 6: ch sc in the same st, sc, sc, sc dc, 2dc, 2dc, dc, sc in the following 5 sts, dc in the following 6 sts, 2dc, sc in the following 6 sts, 2sc, sc, sc, sc, dc in the next 3 sts, sc in the next 6 sts, dc in the next 3 sts, 2dc, 2dc, sc, sc, sc, sl st to the first sc.

Round 7: ch sc in the same st, sc, dc, dc, 3dc, sc in the following 10 sts, dc, dc, 2dc, dc, 2dc, 2dc, sc in the following 9 sts, 2dc, dc in the next 14 sts, 2dc, 2dc, sc in the next 5 sts, sl st to the first ch.

Round 8: ch st in the same st, sc in the following 3 sts, 2sc in the following 3 sts, sc in the following 13 sts, dc, 2dc, 2dc, sc in the next 12 sts, 2sc, sc in the next 16 sts, dc, 2dc, 2dc, sc in the next 6 sts, sl st to the first sc.

Round 9: ch sc in the same st, sc in the following 7 sts, 2dc, dc in the following 16 sts, 3dc, dc, sc in the next 14 sts, 2sc, 2sc, sc in the next 16 sts, 2sc in the next 4 sts, sc in the following 7 sts, sl st to the first sc, fasten off. Embroider eyes and mouth.

Tips

  • Gauge & Sizing: The finished ghost granny square measures about 3.74” x 3.74”.
  • Yarn Weight & Hooks: You can use any yarn and corresponding hook size you prefer. However, using a smaller hook relative to your yarn weight helps create a tighter fabric, which is ideal for colorwork so the black background doesn’t peek through the white stitches.
  • Color Combinations: The classic black and white creates the ultimate ghostly contrast. For extra spookiness, try a glow-in-the-dark white yarn! For a whimsical twist, use a light gray ghost on a deep purple background.
  • If you love this spooky theme, make sure to check out the Free Spade Granny Square Pattern or the Moon Granny Square Pattern for a mystical night sky vibe.

FAQ

What can I make with these squares? These ghostly squares are incredibly versatile! They are perfect for Halloween home décor like festive blankets, cushion covers, trick-or-treat bags, wall hangings, or even coasters for your Halloween party. If you need help figuring out how to join them together, this tutorial on How to Create a Seamless Join for Granny Squares is incredibly helpful!

How do I embroider the face? Using your darning needle and a length of black yarn, simply stitch two small oval or round eyes and a small, jagged or oval mouth directly into the stitches of the white ghost body.

My edges are looking a little wonky. How can I fix this? Graphghan-style colorwork can sometimes cause edges to pull or look uneven. Check out these 3 Secrets to Clean Edges to keep your squares looking perfectly square and professional.

Conclusion

Congratulations on creating your adorable ghost granny square! This spooky little motif makes a perfect building block for festive Halloween home decor and accessories. Share your finished square in the comments below!

title.rendered: Skull and Flower Granny Square

content.rendered:
Crochet meets edgy aesthetics in this unique Skull and Flower Granny Square. This pattern brilliantly combines geometric shapes—a square frame, rounded 3D petals, and a central skull motif—for a truly distinctive design that stands out from traditional squares.

It’s a fantastic project for intermediate crocheters looking to expand their stitch repertoire. The dimensional effect created by the clever stitch combinations in the petals makes this square incredibly satisfying to make. Whether you’re creating a spooky tote bag, a Halloween afghan, or just adding a rebellious touch to your granny square collection, this pattern is a joy to work up.

Materials Needed

  • Yarn of your choice (3 colors)
  • Crochet hook (a 3.00mm hook is used in the example)
  • Darning needle
  • Scissors

Abbreviations Used

  • ch = chain stitch
  • dc = double crochet
  • hdc = half double crochet
  • dtr = double treble crochet
  • sc = single crochet
  • Sl St = slip stitch for joining to different round
  • ch-sp = chain space
  • st = stitch
  • sk = skip
  • inc = increase
  • tl = third loop

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology

Tips & Color Suggestions

The completed granny square measures approximately 5.12 x 5.12 inches. Choosing the right colors can completely change the vibe of your square:

  • Gothic Elegance: Try a black skull, deep purple petals, and a charcoal border for dramatic flair.
  • Soft & Subtle: Consider a cream skull with dusty rose petals on a sage green background for a gentler approach.
  • Halloween Spirit: Orange skull with burgundy petals framed in chocolate brown is perfect for seasonal decorating with a sophisticated spooky style.

Video Tutorial

Follow along with this step-by-step video tutorial to see exactly how to construct the skull center and the beautiful 3D petals!

Pattern Instructions

Round 1: Magic loop, ch3(count as dc),7dc ch5 dc ch3 dc ch5 dc in the loop, sl st to the top of ch3.

Round 2: ch3(count as dc), dc in next gap between 2 dc sts, dc inc in next 5 gaps, dc, 9sc in next ch-sp, sc+ch2+4dc+ch2+sc in next ch-sp, 9sc in next ch-sp, dc in next gap. Sl st to the top of the first ch3, fasten off.

Round 3: Third loop(tl) only. New yarn in the tl of the third dc inc, ch1 as a standing st, sk1, 5dc in the next tl, sk1, sl st, sl st, sk1, 5dc in next tl, sk1, sl st, [sl st, sk1, 5dc in next tl, ch2, sk5, 5dc in next tl, sk1, sl st] repeat 2 times, [sl st, sk1, 5dc in next tl, sk1, sl st] repeat 2 times, join to the first st.

Round 4: sl st in the same st, sc in next dc st, hdc inc, dc inc, hdc inc, sc, sl st to the top of next sl st, [sl st to the top of next sl st, sc, hdc inc, dc inc, hdc inc, sc, sl st to the top of next sl st] repeat 7 times, join to the first st, fasten off.

Round 5: Third loop(tl) only. New yarn in tl of the last sl st, ch3(count as dc), dc, ch3, sk3, sc, hdc, ch3, sk3, dtr, ch3, dtr, ch3, sk3, hdc, sc, ch3, [2dc, ch3, sk3, sc, hdc, ch3, sk3, dtr, ch3, dtr, ch3, sk3, hdc, sc, ch3] repeat 3 times, sl st to the top of the first ch3.

Round 6: ch3(count as dc), dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, 2dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, dc, 2dc+ch3+2dc in next ch-sp, dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, 2dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, [2dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, 2dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, dc, 2dc+ch3+2dc in next ch-sp, dc, 3dc in next ch-sp, 2dc, 3dc in next ch-sp] repeat 3 times, sl st to the top of the first ch3.

Round 7: ch1+sc, 11sc, 2sc+ch1+2sc in corner, 12sc, [12sc, 2sc+ch1+2sc in corner, 12sc] repeat 3 times, sl st to the first sc, fasten off.

Conclusion

Congratulations on finishing your whimsical Skull and Flower Granny Square! This delightful rebel dance between a cheerful flower and a mischievous skull makes for an incredibly unique addition to any project. Share your finished square in the comments below!

More Unique Granny Square Patterns

If you loved this edgy design, you’ll definitely want to check out these other creative granny square patterns:

  • Moon Granny Square Pattern
  • Retro Daisy Granny Square Pattern
  • Enchanted Rose Granny Square: A Free 3D Crochet Pattern

title.rendered: Daisy Granny Square Hair Kerchief Free Crochet Pattern

content.rendered:
Some makes just feel like summer, and this kerchief is exactly that kind of project. Soft cream granny squares — some blooming with puffy little daisies in yellow and white — join together into a triangle that drapes over the hair like something straight out of a countryside picnic. A sage-green scalloped border frames the whole piece, and ties at the corners keep everything snug through a breezy afternoon. Worn over loose waves or braids, it’s cottagecore at its prettiest.

If you love the idea of a triangle head accessory but want to try a different style next, take a look at our modern floral crochet bandana or the boho lace floral crochet bandana for two very different takes on the same wearable shape.

What makes this kerchief especially satisfying to crochet is that it’s really a collection of small, quick wins rather than one long project. Each daisy square comes together as its own little treat — a puffy petal flower that grows outward into a granny square — and once you’ve made a handful, joining them and adding the border goes fast. It’s portable, uses up scraps beautifully, and is the kind of thing you can finish over a weekend without it ever feeling like a chore.

Difficulty level: friendly intermediate. If you’ve made a granny square before, the only new skill here is the puff-stitch daisy center, and it’s much easier than it looks. Gauge is forgiving too, since a kerchief drapes rather than fits closely — making this a low-pressure way to practice motifs and joining techniques.

Materials Needed

Yarn: DK or light worsted (#3) cotton or cotton-blend yarn

  • Cream: approximately 150–200 yards (for the squares and joining)
  • White: a small amount for the daisy petals (under 25 yards)
  • Soft yellow: scraps for the daisy centers
  • Sage green: approximately 40–60 yards (for the border, scallops, and ties)

Hook: US G/6 (4.0mm)

Notions:

  • Yarn needle for joining and weaving in ends
  • Scissors
  • Stitch markers (helpful while joining squares)
  • Rust-proof pins for blocking
  • Measuring tape

Abbreviations Used (US Terms)

  • ch — chain
  • sc — single crochet
  • dc — double crochet
  • sl st — slip stitch
  • st(s) — stitch(es)
  • sp — space
  • MR — magic ring
  • puff — puff stitch: (yarn over, insert hook, pull up a loop) 3–4 times into the same stitch or space, yarn over and pull through all the loops on your hook, then chain 1 to close
  • rep — repeat

Pattern Notes

This pattern uses US crochet terminology throughout.

The kerchief is built from individual granny square motifs — a mix of daisy squares and plain squares — each worked in the round, then joined together into a triangle layout and finished off with a green scallop border and corner ties.

Gauge here is fairly relaxed: each finished square should measure about 3 inches (7.5cm). Getting the exact gauge matters less than staying consistent — squares that are all the same size will join up cleanly no matter the precise measurement. At 3-inch squares, the layout below produces a kerchief around 15 inches (38cm) across the front edge, which fits most adults comfortably.

Layout: the squares form a triangle — a row of 4 across the front edge, then 3, then 2, then 1 at the back point, for 10 squares total. You can mix the daisy and plain squares however you like; using 6 daisy squares and 4 plain squares, scattered throughout, matches the look shown in the photos.

Stitch counts appear in parentheses at the end of each round.

Finished size: approximately 15 inches (38cm) along the front edge and 11 inches (28cm) from front to back point, plus the ties. See the FAQ section below for resizing notes.

Pattern Instructions

The Daisy Square (make 6)

Round 1 (center): With yellow yarn, make a magic ring, ch 1, work 8 sc into the ring, pull it closed, and join with a sl st to the first sc. (8 sts) Fasten off the yellow.

Round 2 (petals): Join white yarn in any stitch. Work [a puff stitch into the next stitch, ch 1] eight times around, then join to the top of the first puff. (8 puff petals) Pull each puff stitch’s loops up generously so the petals sit plump and rounded, just like a real daisy. Fasten off the white.

Round 3 (squaring it up): Join cream yarn in any ch-1 space between the petals. Ch 3 (counts as your first dc), work 2 more dc into the same space; in the next space work 3 dc; in the following space work (3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc) to form a corner. Repeat this sequence around so that four evenly spaced ch-1 spaces become your corners, with plain 3-dc groups filling the spaces between them, then join.

Round 4: Slip stitch over to the first corner space. Ch 3, then work (2 dc, ch 2, 3 dc) into that corner space. Work 3 dc into each side space along the edge, and (3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc) into each corner space as you go. Repeat all the way around and join. This completes one daisy square, approximately 3 inches across.

Fasten off, leaving a tail for joining later.

The Plain Square (make 4)

Round 1: With cream yarn, make a magic ring, ch 3 (counts as dc), work 2 more dc into the ring, ch 2, then 3 dc, ch 2 — repeat this two more times, then join. (4 corner groups)

Rounds 2–3: Slip stitch to the corner space, ch 3, work (2 dc, ch 2, 3 dc) into the corner; 3 dc into each side space; (3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc) into each corner. Repeat around, joining at the end of each round. This produces a square matching the size of the daisy squares, approximately 3 inches across.

If your plain squares end up smaller than your daisy squares, add a round of sc around the plain ones until the sizes match — consistent sizing matters more than matching round counts.

Fasten off, leaving tails for joining.

Joining Into the Kerchief Triangle

Lay your squares out in the triangle formation: a front row of 4 squares, then 3, then 2, then 1 at the back point, scattering the daisy squares among the plain ones however looks best to you.

To join, use cream yarn and a yarn needle to whip stitch through the back loops, or use a sl-st or sc join instead. Seam the squares row by row first, then join the rows together, keeping your tension consistent throughout so the finished piece drapes evenly. Don’t worry about the stepped, diagonal edges along the sides of the triangle at this stage — the border will smooth those out.

The Border & Scallops (Sage Green)

Round 1 (smoothing round): Join green yarn at a front corner. Work sc evenly all the way around the triangle — along the front edge and both diagonal edges — placing enough stitches across each square and 3 sc at the outer corners to keep the piece lying flat. Along the stepped diagonal edges, ease your stitch placement so the steps round out into a smooth line.

Round 2 (scallops): Sc in the next stitch, skip 2 stitches, work 5 dc into the next stitch, skip 2 stitches — repeat this around both diagonal edges. Along the straight front edge, you can either continue the same scallop repeat or switch to plain sc for a flatter edge near the hairline; working scallops all the way around matches the look in the original photos, so continue the repeat there too if you’d like the same finish. Join and fasten off.

The Ties

At each end of the front edge, join green yarn and work a chain of 40–50 stitches for a simple tie. For something sturdier, you can instead work a slip-stitch cord or a narrow 3-stitch sc strip about 10–12 inches long. Fasten off and weave in the ends. The ties knot together beneath the hair at the nape of the neck.

Tips & Tricks

  • Make all your squares first, then compare them. Stack the finished squares together — any that are off in size will show up immediately, and it’s much easier to add an equalizing round now than to fight an uneven join later.
  • Plump up your puff stitches. Pull each loop of the puff stitch up tall — about half an inch — before closing it. Skimpy loops make flat petals, while generous loops make the daisies look full and rounded.
  • Block your squares before joining. Pin each one out to 3 inches and let it set. Blocked motifs join together like neat tiles instead of fighting each other into odd shapes.
  • Join with matching tension. A joining row that’s tighter than the squares themselves will pucker the whole kerchief. Keep your joins loose and even to preserve a soft drape over the head.
  • Ease the diagonal edges as you border. The stepped edge of a squared-off triangle usually needs slightly fewer border stitches than you’d expect — if your border starts to ruffle, pull it back and space your sc round a bit tighter.
  • Try it on before adding the ties. Drape the bordered triangle over your head and check the front-edge length. If it feels too narrow or too wide, adjust the tie length to compensate, or add an extra round of sc along the front edge.

 

 

 

Finishing

Weave in all your ends — this motif-based project generates plenty of tails, so bury each one in two directions through matching-color stitches and trim close.

Wet-block or steam-block the finished kerchief flat, pinning the scallops open so each little scallop sets crisply into shape.

Attach or finish off the ties, knot the ends, and trim.

To wear: drape it over the crown of your head with the point sitting at the back, tie it beneath your hair at the nape, and pull a few loose strands free for that easy, effortless look.

FAQ

How do I resize it for a child or a larger head? You have two main levers: square size (a smaller hook and finer yarn will shrink every square) and layout (a smaller 3-2-1 triangle made from six squares gives a sweet child’s size, while adding a fifth square to the front row and a fourth row overall creates a more generous adult drape). Check the front-edge length against an ear-to-ear-over-the-crown measurement, plus a little extra ease.

My daisy squares and plain squares came out different sizes — help? That’s completely normal, since puff-stitch rounds tend to work up denser than plain granny rounds. Add an equalizing round of sc (or another granny round) to whichever squares are smaller until the sizes match. Matching size matters more than matching round count.

The border is ruffling and the kerchief won’t lie flat — what went wrong? This is almost always caused by too many stitches in the smoothing round along the diagonal edges. Unravel the border, rework the sc round with slightly fewer, more evenly spaced stitches, and block again — it should lie flat quickly after that.

Can I make it in other colors? Absolutely. Keep the daisies white and yellow and swap the cream base for sage, dusty blue, or lavender, or go for a full meadow look with mixed pastel squares. A neutral border ties any color combination together nicely.

Closing

And there’s your daisy kerchief — ten little squares that add up to one of the most charming things you’ll wear all summer. Every daisy square is its own quick, satisfying win, and the whole project stays small enough to carry around in a tote bag. Make one in cream, and don’t be surprised when everyone who sees it asks for one of their own — this is that kind of make.

Looking for more bandana and kerchief inspiration? Check out our full roundup of 18 free crochet bandana patterns for beginners for even more styles to try next.

title.rendered: 18 Free Crochet Bandana Patterns for Beginners

content.rendered:
Table of Contents

Toggle
  • 1. Granny Bandana
  • 2. Crochet Head Kerchief
  • 3. Tunisian Bandana
  • 4. Granny Square Bandana
  • 5. Pink Bandana
  • 6. Shell Stitch Bandana
  • 7. Daisy Bandana
  • 8. Sweetheart Bandana
  • 9. Lilly Bandana
  • 10. Vintage Bandana
  • 11. DIY Leaf Bandana
  • 12. DIY Granny Square Pattern
  • 13. Sunflower Bandana Pattern
  • 14. Fringe Bandana
  • 15. Simple Hair Accessory
  • 16. Picot Crochet Bandana
  • 17. Triangle Bandana
  • 18. Handcrafted Head Scarf
  • Final Thoughts

A crochet bandana might just be the fastest way to fix a bad hair day while adding a handmade touch to your look. Whether you want a triangle headscarf for the beach, a granny-square style piece for festival season, or something delicate enough for everyday wear, there’s a pattern out there for every skill level and style.

This roundup pulls together 18 beginner-friendly bandana patterns — classic shapes, trendy motifs, and a few unexpected twists — so you can find your next quick project without digging through dozens of sites yourself.

 

1. Granny Bandana

 

 

 

This breezy summer piece comes together in about 30 minutes flat, making it a great last-minute fix for a rough hair day. It’s worked using two different stitch methods and finished off with a slightly ruffled, scalloped edge plus simple ties. Get the pattern here.

2. Crochet Head Kerchief

 

 

Built with basic double crochet stitches, this triangle-shaped bandana is designed with non-curling borders and lightweight yarn — perfect for keeping the sun off your head without feeling heavy. Swap in your favorite yarn color for an easy personal touch. Get the pattern here.

3. Tunisian Bandana

 

 

A great pick if you’re curious about Tunisian crochet but not ready for anything complex — this design relies mainly on simple and purl stitches, with no strict gauge required. Work up a small swatch first if you want to double-check your tension. Get the pattern here.

4. Granny Square Bandana

 

 

A tidy, wearable take on the classic granny square, made with just DK yarn, a 4.0mm hook, a yarn needle, and scissors. It’s a nice low-fuss project if you already have granny square basics down and want to turn them into something wearable. Get the pattern here.

5. Pink Bandana

 

 

Light and airy, this triangle headscarf is worked in cotton yarn, making it especially well-suited to spring and summer wear. It’s a versatile pick for the beach, an outdoor festival, or just running errands in warm weather. Get the pattern here.

6. Shell Stitch Bandana

 

 

Leaning into a cottagecore look, this bandana uses the shell stitch as its main texture for a soft, boho feel. It’s a great pattern for beginners who want to practice foundational shell-stitch skills while making something they’ll actually wear. Get the pattern here.

7. Daisy Bandana

 

 

If cheerful floral motifs are your thing, this daisy-inspired bandana is an easy, approachable project for beginners who are ready for a slightly more adventurous pattern. The daisy detail gives it a fresh, spring-ready feel. Get the pattern here.

8. Sweetheart Bandana

 

 

This heart-motif design is a good option once you’re comfortable with basic bandana shaping and ready to build advanced-beginner skills. It uses bobbins to keep the color work clean, along with a few other simple supplies. Get the pattern here.

9. Lilly Bandana

 

 

Another cottagecore-inspired piece, this lily-themed bandana is refreshingly simple to work up while still looking polished once finished. It sits nicely on the head and makes a sweet everyday accessory. Get the pattern here.

10. Vintage Bandana

 

 

With a delicate, variegated look, this bandana brings in a bit of old-world charm. It’s a relaxing project that works well as background stitching while you watch TV or unwind after a long day. Get the pattern here.

11. DIY Leaf Bandana

 

 

Simple, pretty, and easy to wear on repeat — this leaf-motif design uses just a handful of basic stitches: chain, slip stitch, single crochet, and treble crochet. It’s the kind of low-effort, high-reward project you’ll want to make more than once. Get the pattern here.

12. DIY Granny Square Pattern

 

 

Made from a cluster of small, colorful granny squares, this fun bandana taps into current trend territory while staying totally beginner-friendly. It’s an easy choice for festivals, beach days, or casual weekend outings. Get the pattern here.

13. Sunflower Bandana Pattern

 

 

Sunflowers are the ultimate warm-weather motif, and this bandana makes the most of that cheerful energy. The stitching is straightforward, the finished look is eye-catching, and it’s the kind of piece that tends to draw compliments every time you wear it. Get the pattern here.

14. Fringe Bandana

 

 

Built from a cluster of small, colorful granny-square flowers, this design gets an extra boost of personality from the fringe detailing along the back edge. It’s a fun way to combine floral motifs with a little movement and texture. Get the pattern here.

15. Simple Hair Accessory

 

 

This one’s ideal if you’ve got leftover yarn scraps to use up. The pattern comes with a detailed, easy-to-follow tutorial that’s approachable even if you’ve genuinely never picked up a crochet hook before — and there’s a video to walk you through it step by step. Get the pattern here.

16. Picot Crochet Bandana

 

 

Featuring dainty picot detailing, this bandana pattern comes in three different sizes, so you can pick your fit or even make a few in different sizes as matching accessories for family or friends. Get the pattern here.

17. Triangle Bandana

 

 

Fast and genuinely beginner-friendly, this triangle granny-stitch bandana can be finished in under three hours — even if you’ve never crocheted before. Wear it as a headscarf, or tie it around your waist for a completely different look. Get the pattern here.

18. Handcrafted Head Scarf

 

 

Worked in soft milk cotton yarn with a 3.5mm hook, this minimalist bandana keeps things simple while still feeling special, thanks to two small flower accents attached at the ends of the ties. A little detail that goes a long way. Get the pattern here.

Final Thoughts

From quick 30-minute makes to slightly more detailed floral and granny-square designs, this list has a beginner-friendly bandana pattern for pretty much any mood, season, or occasion. Pick one that matches your current skill level, grab your favorite yarn, and you’ll have a new handmade accessory ready in no time.

title.rendered: Boho Lace Floral Crochet Bandana Free Pattern

content.rendered:
This triangular boho bandana works up from the top point downward, growing outward row by row into a clean isosceles triangle. At its heart sits a delicate floral mandala motif, surrounded by open lacework, a scalloped pointed edge, and a beaded fringe along the base. The finished piece drapes beautifully and works equally well as a headscarf, kerchief, or neck accessory, with corner ties you can adjust for a comfortable fit on almost anyone.

The shaping stays approachable throughout — simple increases paired with V-stitches, shells, and picots build the floral look naturally as the triangle grows, so you’re never fighting complicated shaping instructions.

If you liked our modern floral motif crochet bandana, this lacier boho version is a great next project to try.

Why This Pattern Is Worth Making

The open, airy lace structure keeps this bandana lightweight and breathable — ideal for warm-weather wear or layering over a summer outfit. Along the way you’ll practice building a central floral motif while keeping your triangle increases clean, then finish with a professional scalloped border and beaded fringe for that elevated boho look.

Because the V-stitches, shells, and picots repeat in a predictable rhythm as the piece grows, you can relax into the stitch pattern instead of tracking complex shaping. It stitches up fast in lightweight cotton, and there’s plenty of room to make it your own with size, bead, or fringe adjustments.

What You’ll Need

Yarn: 70–90 grams (220–280 yards) of fingering weight (#1) or DK weight (#3) cotton or cotton-blend yarn. Good options include a mercerized cotton like Scheepjes Catona (about 136 yards per 50g ball) or a budget-friendly cotton 8/4 in cream or off-white.

Hook: 3.5mm or 4.0mm — go with the larger size if you want an airier, more open drape.

Notions:

  • 12–18 wooden beads (8–12mm)
  • 24–36 small metallic or seed beads
  • Tapestry needle
  • Scissors
  • Blocking pins and mat (strongly recommended)

Gauge: 18 dc and 9 rows = 4 inches (10cm) in the main lace pattern, measured after blocking. Gauge has some flexibility here since this is an accessory, not a fitted garment.

Choosing the Right Yarn

A smooth, lightweight cotton or cotton-blend yarn gives you the best drape and the crispest stitch definition for this lace design. Mercerized cotton in particular produces sharp stitches with a soft sheen while staying breathable — exactly what you want in a headscarf or kerchief.

Stick to smooth, lighter-weight cottons rather than fuzzy or heavily textured yarns, which tend to blur the floral motif and hide the scalloped edge detail. Whatever you choose, always swatch first — cotton has a tendency to stretch a little once it’s blocked, which actually works in this pattern’s favor by opening up the lace even more.

Size and Fit Details

Finished size:

  • Base width: 48–55cm (19–22 inches)
  • Point-to-base depth: 28–32cm (11–12.5 inches)
  • Ties: 50–70cm each, and adjustable

This one-size design comfortably fits most adults as either a headscarf or a neckerchief. Because the triangle is built row by row, you can easily customize the depth — stop 4–5 rows earlier than written for a smaller version that works well as a teen size or a neck scarf.

Blocking is what really brings this pattern to life: the lace relaxes and opens up dramatically, revealing the scalloped edge and floral center in full. Wet blocking with pins gives the crispest, most polished result.

Before You Start

This bandana is worked flat, in rows, starting from the top center point and increasing outward into a triangle shape. The central floral motif isn’t a separate piece — it builds naturally out of the shell and picot placement as you work through the increase rows.

Keep your tension loose to preserve that open, lacy look; if your stitches feel tight or the fabric starts to pucker, size up your hook by half a millimeter. Every 5–6 rows, lay the piece flat and check that it’s widening evenly on both sides.

Don’t skip blocking — this is the step where the lace truly opens up and the floral center and scalloped edge come into focus. Pinning the damp piece into a precise triangle gives you the cleanest finished shape. If you like, place stitch markers along both increasing edges to help you track your increases as you go, and save the beaded fringe for last so you can fine-tune the spacing once your border is complete.

Most crocheters find the repeating lace sections easy to memorize after the first 8 rows or so. Take your time through the central floral section in particular — that’s where the mandala detail really shines.

Stitches and Abbreviations Used

US terms:

  • ch – chain
  • sl st – slip stitch
  • sc – single crochet
  • dc – double crochet
  • tr – treble crochet
  • sp – space
  • st(s) – stitch(es)

Special stitches:

  • V-st – (dc, ch 2, dc) worked in the same stitch or space
  • Shell – (2 dc, ch 2, 2 dc) worked in the same stitch or space
  • Picot – ch 3, sl st into the 3rd chain from the hook
  • Floral Cluster – (3 dc, ch 3, 3 dc) worked in the same space, forming the petal shapes in the central motif

Repeats are marked with asterisks (**). Turning chains count as your first stitch unless the pattern says otherwise, and for the lightest lace, always work into chain spaces from the previous row rather than into the stitches themselves.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Work from the top point (which sits at the center back of the head) downward, increasing at both edges every row to build the triangle. Keep your tension relaxed throughout for the best lace effect.

Foundation and Central Floral Build

Row 1: Ch 5, work (dc, ch 2, dc) into the 5th chain from the hook — this is your first V-st. Turn. (1 V-st)

Row 2: Ch 3 (counts as dc), work a V-st into the ch-2 space, dc into the top of the turning chain. Turn. (2 V-sts)

Row 3: Ch 3, dc into the first dc, ch 1, work a Shell into the next ch-2 space, ch 1, dc into the last dc. Turn.

Row 4: Ch 3, dc into the first dc, ch 1, (dc, ch 1, dc) into the next ch-1 space, Shell into the ch-2 space of the previous Shell, ch 1, (dc, ch 1, dc) into the next ch-1 space, dc into the last dc. Turn.

Row 5: Ch 3, dc into the first dc, ch 1, dc into the next dc, ch 1 repeating out to the center. Work a Floral Cluster — (3 dc, ch 3, 3 dc) — into the center ch-2 space. Chain 1, then mirror the dc, ch 1 repeat back out to the end, finishing with a dc into the last dc. Turn.

Rows 6–10: Keep increasing at both edges with your ch 3, dc, ch 1 repeat pattern. In the central Floral Cluster space, build out the motif further by adding (3 dc, picot, 3 dc) groups on the odd-numbered rows — this is what creates the signature mandala look at the center. Check your width every few rows to make sure both sides are growing evenly.

Main Body Lace

Rows 11–22 (or until you reach your desired depth): Ch 3 (or ch 4 for a taller, airier lace), then work a V-st or (dc, ch 1) mesh pattern across the row, dropping in the occasional Shell or small Floral Cluster every 6–8 stitches for scattered floral accents. Increase at both edges each row by adding a dc plus ch 1 at the start and end. Stop once your base measures approximately 48–55cm across.

The fabric should feel light and drapey at this stage. If it starts to curl, your tension is likely too tight — move up to a larger hook.

Scalloped Border

Work this along both long sides and the base: sc into the next stitch or space, skip 2–3 stitches, work a Shell — (2 dc, ch 2, 2 dc, picot, 2 dc) — into the next space, skip 2–3 stitches, and repeat this sequence around all three sides. Adjust your skip counts slightly as needed to keep the scallop points evenly spaced.

Ties

At each top corner, attach your yarn and chain 55–70. Work one row of sc back along the chain for extra strength, or simply leave the ties as plain chains and thread beads near the ends instead.

Assembly and Finishing

Weave in every end securely with your tapestry needle.

Blocking: Wet the bandana thoroughly and gently squeeze out the excess water, then pin it into a precise triangle shape on your blocking mat and let it dry fully. This step is what transforms the lace and sharpens the scalloped edge.

Beaded fringe: Cut 15–20 lengths of yarn, each 20–25cm long. Thread one large wooden bead plus 2–3 small metallic beads onto each strand, fold the strand in half, and attach it at every scallop point (or every 2–3cm along the base) using a lark’s head knot. Trim the ends evenly once you’re done.

Your finished bandana should feel sturdy but delicate — and like most cotton pieces, it’ll only get softer and drapier with wear and washing.

If you enjoy triangle-shaped accessories like this one, our elegant winter scarf crochet pattern and easy fall crochet scarf pattern are worth adding to your queue too.

Easy Variations to Try

Smaller version: Work only 18–20 total rows before starting the border. This brings the base width down to roughly 38–42cm — a good fit for teens or as a compact neck scarf.

Larger, shawl-style piece: Keep working the main body lace until your base reaches 70–80cm (usually around 28–32 rows total), and add a few extra Floral Clusters through the body for a denser mandala effect.

Color ideas: Stick with a solid cream as written, or introduce subtle stripes by switching colors every 4–5 rows in the body. A variegated fingering-weight yarn also shows off beautifully in this stitch pattern for a rainbow boho effect.

Yarn weight swaps: A sport-weight yarn with a 4.5mm hook gives you a drapier, larger finished piece, while fingering weight with a 3.5mm hook produces a more delicate, refined lace.

Fringe variations: Skip the beads entirely for a simple tassel look, use longer 30cm strands for more dramatic movement, or bead only every other scallop for something lighter.

You can also turn the corner ties into a continuous lace tie by working the chain as a foundation row and adding picots along its length.

If you’re in the mood for more color-play projects after this one, take a look at our color block crochet super scarf pattern.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

Piece curling or feels too tight: Size up your hook by half a millimeter and consciously loosen your tension, especially on chain stitches. Blocking will also help relax the fabric afterward.

Stitch counts not matching: Double check your increases at the start and end of each row — both edges should be adding the same number of stitches. If they’ve drifted apart, unravel back to the last correct row and re-mark your edges before continuing.

Lace looking flat or dense: Make sure you’re working into the chain spaces rather than the stitches themselves. Using a longer turning chain (ch 4 instead of ch 3) on later rows also helps create taller, airier stitches.

Uneven scalloped border: Adjust how many stitches you skip between shells as you go — it’s completely normal to skip 2 in some spots and 3 in others to keep the scallop points looking even.

Beads sliding or fringe looking uneven: Tie a small knot just below each bead, or add a tiny dab of fabric glue to hold the knot in place. Trim all the fringe strands at once while the piece is still pinned flat for the most even length.

Finished piece smaller than expected: Cotton yarn grows noticeably during wet blocking, so always block the piece before you add the fringe to get an accurate final size.

Next-Level Tips

Once you’re comfortable with the triangle increases and the floral cluster technique, you can scale this same construction up into a full triangular shawl — just keep working the body rows and repeat the scalloped border along all three edges. The same central-motif approach also translates nicely into rectangular wraps or baby blankets when worked straight across in rows without edge increases.

Want to design your own spin on it? Swap the Floral Clusters in the center for granny squares or a different shell arrangement, or extend the scalloped border into a full edging you could use on other garments.

The main body’s lace repeat also works well in market bags or lightweight scarves — and that beaded fringe technique is an easy way to add boho detail to towels, blankets, or finished garment edges.

If you enjoy working with granny-style motifs and clusters, our sunburst granny square blanket pattern and chunky daisy blanket pattern use similar techniques on a bigger scale.

Caring for Your Bandana

Since it’s made from cotton, this bandana is low-maintenance. Hand wash in lukewarm water with a mild detergent, or machine wash on a gentle cycle inside a mesh bag. Lay it flat to dry so it holds its shape and doesn’t stretch out of proportion.

Skip the fabric softener — it tends to weigh down delicate lace. After washing, re-block the piece while it’s still damp to refresh the scalloped edges and floral detail, and store it folded flat or hanging to keep the beads and fringe from creasing.

Final Thoughts

This boho lace floral bandana pairs eye-catching openwork with genuine everyday wearability. The clear, repeating increases and motifs make it a satisfying project for building confidence with lace crochet techniques.

Take your time with the blocking and beaded fringe steps in particular — they’re what push this piece from simply handmade to polished and finished. Once complete, you’ll likely find yourself reaching for it all season long.

For more small wearable projects, check out our simple crochet scarf pattern and crochet cable scarf pattern — both make great companion pieces to this bandana.

title.rendered: Modern Crochet Bandana Pattern That Feels Fresh & Minimal

content.rendered:
A crochet bandana is one of those small accessories that can completely change the feel of an outfit. Worn as a headscarf, tied around the neck, or clipped onto a bag, it adds a handmade touch without feeling fussy or overdone. This modern floral motif design keeps things clean and minimal, so it pairs easily with everyday looks while still showing off real handmade texture.

If you enjoy quick accessory projects like this one, you might also like our simple crochet scarf pattern or the elegant winter scarf crochet pattern for more wearable makes that come together fast.

Prefer to follow along visually? Here’s a helpful video walkthrough you can watch alongside the written pattern below.

What You’ll Need

  • A 3mm crochet hook
  • Lightweight cotton yarn
  • Scissors and a yarn needle for weaving in ends

Gauge: one complete floral motif measures roughly 2 inches across.

Motif count for a medium headband: 8 full motifs plus 2 half motifs.

Step 1: Make the Full Motif

Round 1 — Build the base circle

Start with a magic ring and chain 4 (this stands in for your first double crochet plus a chain-1 space). Into the ring, work a double crochet followed by a chain-2 space, and repeat this sequence seven more times, giving you 8 double crochets and 8 chain-2 spaces total. Pull the tail to close the ring, then slip stitch into the third chain of your starting chain-4 to join the round.

Stitch count: 8 dc, 8 chain-2 spaces.

 

 

Round 2 — Shape the petals

Slip stitch into the first chain-2 space and chain 5 to set up your first petal. To build the cluster stitch in that same space: yarn over, insert your hook into the space, pull up a loop, yarn over and draw through two loops — repeat this four times so you end up with five loops sitting on your hook. Yarn over one final time and pull through all five loops together, then chain 1 to lock the cluster in place.

Chain 4 and move to the next chain-2 space, repeating the same cluster stitch there. Continue around until every space has a petal, then slip stitch into the top of your very first cluster to close the round.

Stitch count: 8 petal clusters with 8 connecting chain-4 spaces.

Step 2: Join Your Motifs As You Go

Joining a single edge

When you start a new motif and reach the fourth petal, swap the usual chain-4 for this: chain 2, slip stitch into the matching chain-4 space on the neighboring motif, then chain 2 again. Finish the cluster in your current motif’s space as normal and keep going.

Joining at a corner (double edge)

Where three motifs come together, insert your hook through the shared chain-4 space of both neighboring motifs at once, pull up a loop, and slip stitch. Then complete the cluster stitch in your current space before continuing.

Step 3: Make the Half Motifs for the Edges

Half motifs give the bandana its tapered, triangular ends.

Round 1

Magic ring, chain 4, then work a double crochet plus chain-2 space six times (instead of eight) into the ring. Close by pulling the tail tight and slip stitching into your starting chain to join.

Stitch count: 6 dc, 6 chain-2 spaces.

Round 2

Work petals the same way as the full motif, just across six spaces instead of eight. After your last petal, chain 2 and slip stitch into the corner of the neighboring motif to attach it, then fasten off and weave in your ends.

Step 4: Lay Out and Assemble

Arrange your motifs like this for a triangular bandana shape (scale the numbers up or down for a different size):

Row Full Motifs Half Motifs Join Type
Top 3 0 Single edge
Middle 2 0 Double edge
Bottom 1 2 (one each side) Double edge

Attach the half motifs along the bottom row edges, matching them up with the full motifs beside them using the double-edge join.

Step 5: Add the Border and Ties

Join your yarn at any point along the outer edge of the assembled piece. Work 2–3 double crochets into each chain-4 space as you go around the entire perimeter for a clean, finished edge.

At each top corner, chain 60 to form the ties, then slip stitch back along the chain to give the ties a bit more body and thickness.

Once assembled, give the bandana a light steam block or gentle iron so the motifs sit flat and the stitch detail really stands out.

 

 

Tips for a Smoother Make

  • Join as you go. It’s faster than sewing motifs together afterward and gives you neater seams.
  • Play with color. Alternating shades between motifs can turn this into a much bolder, statement piece.
  • Watch your edging count. Adjust how many double crochets you work per space if your border starts to ruffle or pull tight.

This floral motif bandana is a great small-scale project if you’re between bigger makes — and once you’ve got the motif join-as-you-go technique down, it carries over nicely into other granny-style projects like our sunburst granny square blanket or the chunky daisy blanket pattern. And if you’re building out a matching set, our crochet cable scarf pattern makes a cozy companion piece.

title.rendered: Summer Days Daisy Bag

content.rendered:
There is something undeniably special about crocheting daisy granny squares. They bring a bright, nostalgic charm that instantly transports you back to simpler times, making them incredibly joyful to stitch up. This beautiful shoulder bag takes that classic motif and transforms it into a highly functional, everyday accessory.

The Summer Days Daisy Bag is a fantastic project for confident beginners looking to expand their skills. By seaming together 15 colorful granny squares in a clever layout, you will create a stunning bag that is perfect for keeping your essentials close while enjoying hands-free convenience on warm days out.

Materials Needed

  • 4 skeins of 24/7 Cotton (worsted weight level 4 yarn)
  • Color A: 116 g/216 yds (Succulent) – 2 skeins
  • Color B: 42 g/78 yds (Ecru) – 1 skein
  • Color C: 24 g/45 yds (Goldenrod) – 1 skein
  • 2.75 mm and 3.75 mm crochet hooks
  • Yarn needle (bent tip helpful for attaching)
  • Lock ring stitch markers
  • Steamer (optional for blocking granny squares)
  • Small purse organizer insert (optional to add zipper closure and compartments; dimensions: Length: 9″/23 cm, Height: 5.9″/15 cm)

Abbreviations Used

  • Magic Ring (MR): Make a loop. Hold yarn where ends cross. Insert hook into loop and pull up working yarn. Yarn over and pull through. Work subsequent stitches in magic ring and then pull tight to close.
  • Beginning cluster: Ch 2, [YO, insert hook in st, YO, pull up a loop, YO, draw through 2 loops], rep 3 times in same st, YO, draw through 4 loops on hook.
  • Cluster: [YO, insert hook in st, YO, draw up a loop, YO, draw through 2 loops on hook], rep 4 times in same st, YO, draw through 5 loops on hook.
  • Half double crochet decrease: YO, insert hook into both indicated gaps. YO, pull through first 2 loops. YO, pull through remaining 3 loops.
  • Invisible single crochet decrease (worked across 3 stitches in this pattern): Insert hook into front loops of next 3 stitches. YO, pull through 3 loops. YO, pull through both loops.
  • Invisible slip stitch decrease (worked across 3 stitches in this pattern): Insert hook into front loops of next 3 stitches. YO, pull through all loops.

This pattern uses USA crochet terminology

Pattern Notes

This bag is constructed of 15 granny squares seamed together in a special way to form the shape. Color A serves as the background frame, Color B creates the petals, and Color C forms the daisy center.

The daisy granny square consists of 5 rounds: Rounds 1 and 2 make the center of the daisy using single crochet, Round 3 forms the petals using clusters, and Rounds 4 and 5 build the background frame using half double crochet and double crochet stitches.

You can crochet over the yarn tails when switching colors for a neater finish. Once all squares are complete, they are laid out in a specific arrangement and seamed together using a slip stitch method. Stitches are then picked up along the top edge to form a lovely eyelet top edging and strap. Adjust the length of the strap based on where you want the bag to hang, keeping in mind that it will hang lower once filled with items. Blocking your squares helps relax the fibers and gives a smooth finish, and this bag is technically reversible depending on which side of the stitches you prefer to show!

Pattern Instructions

Daisy Granny Square

 

 

With Color C (Goldenrod),

Using 3.75 mm hook,

Round 1: 12 sc in Magic Ring. Sl st to first sc. (12 sts)

R2: Chain 1, sc in same st. Sc around. Sl st to first sc. Fasten off. (12 sts)

With Color B (Ecru),

R3: Join with sl st in any sc. Work beginning cluster, chain 3. Work cluster in next sc, chain 3 around. Slip stitch to top of beg cluster. Fasten off. (12 clusters and 12 ch-3 spaces)

With Color C (Succulent),

R4: Join with slip st in any ch-3 space. Chain 3 (counts as 1 dc), 2 dc, chain 2, 3 dc in same space. Work 3 hdc in each of next 2 ch-3 spaces. [Work 3 dc, chain 2, 3 dc in next ch-3 space. Work 3 hdc in each of next 2 ch-3 spaces.] Repeat everything between square brackets [ ] 2 more times. Slip stitch to top of chain 3. (48 sts and 4 ch-2 spaces).

R5: Chain 2 (counts as 1 hdc). Work 1 hdc in next st. Skip next st, 2 hdc, chain 2, 2 hdc in chain-2 space. [Skip next st, hdc across until reach st before Ch 2 space (10 hdc). Skip next st, 2 hdc, chain 2, 2 hdc in ch-2 space.]. Repeat everything between square brackets [ ] 2 more times. Skip next st, hdc 8. Slip st to top of chain 2. Fasten off. (56 sts and 4 ch-2 spaces).

Note: Crochet 15 granny squares in total. You can block the squares to give them defined edges and to smooth out the stitches.

Assembly and Strap

To complete the bag, assemble the 15 granny squares together using a slip stitch seaming technique. After the bag body is seamed, crochet the top edging and strap by picking up stitches along the top edge and working half double crochets separated by chain 1’s for the eyelet detail. A round of single crochet is then worked along one side of the top edging and strap, followed by a round of slip stitches to strengthen and widen the strap. Repeat on the other side, working the special decrease stitches at the bottom of the V so the stitches do not bunch up.

Conclusion

Congratulations on completing your Summer Days Daisy Bag! This nostalgic, cheery design is the perfect handmade accessory for sunny days out. Share your finished bag in the comments below!

More Crochet Patterns to Try

If you loved making this granny square bag, you might enjoy these other fun projects:

  • Flower Granny Square Bag Crochet Pattern
  • Daisy Granny Square Free Crochet Pattern
  • Mastering the Basic Granny Square: A Timeless Crochet Pattern
